subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Energy and Energy Transfer
subtitle: Reading passages and questions about energy transfer, heat, conservation, systems, and evidence.
description: This pack helps students trace how energy is stored, transferred, and transformed in everyday systems. It includes key vocabulary, evidence-based reasoning, heat transfer methods, conservation of energy, material properties, real-world examples, data interpretation, and common misconceptions.

data.sourcePassage: Energy is not a material object that can be held by itself. In science, energy is a property of matter and systems that helps explain change. When a skateboard speeds up, a lamp glows, ice melts, a guitar string vibrates, or a phone screen lights up, energy is involved. Scientists usually begin by identifying the system they are studying. The system might be one object, such as a ball, or a group of objects, such as a battery, wire, and bulb. Then they ask where energy was stored at the start, where it transferred, and what evidence shows a change. Evidence can include motion, a temperature change, light, sound, a changed shape, or a reading from a measuring tool.

data.sourcePassage: In everyday speech, people often use heat and temperature as if they mean the same thing. In science, they are different. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance. Thermal energy is related to particle motion and the amount of matter present. Heat means thermal energy transferring from a warmer object to a cooler object. If an ice cube is placed in warm water, thermal energy transfers from the water to the ice. The ice warms and may melt, while the water cools. This transfer happens because there is a temperature difference. A bathtub of warm water can contain more thermal energy than a small cup of very hot tea because the bathtub contains much more matter.

data.sourcePassage: Heat transfer can happen by conduction, convection, or radiation. Conduction happens through direct contact. Particles collide or interact and pass energy along, which is why a metal spoon can warm when it sits in hot soup. Convection happens in fluids, which are liquids and gases. Warmer fluid often becomes less dense and rises while cooler fluid sinks, creating currents that transfer thermal energy. Radiation is energy transfer by electromagnetic waves. It does not require direct contact or matter. Energy from the Sun reaches Earth by radiation through space. These three processes often happen together in real systems, such as a toaster warming bread or a thermos trying to slow heat transfer.

data.sourcePassage: Energy transformation means energy changes from one form to another. A flashlight transforms chemical energy stored in a battery into electrical energy in a circuit, then into light energy and thermal energy at the bulb or LED. A falling ball transforms gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy as it speeds up. The law of conservation of energy says energy cannot be created or destroyed. This can be difficult to notice because useful energy often spreads out into the surroundings. A bouncing ball does not bounce forever because some energy becomes sound and thermal energy in the ball, ground, and air. The energy is still conserved, but less of it remains as useful motion energy.

data.sourceTitle: Using Data to Explain Energy Transfer
data.targetTitle: Using Data to Explain Energy Transfer
data.sourcePassage: A class tested how cup color affects warming in sunlight. A white cup and a black cup each held 100 mL of water and started at 20°C. After 30 minutes in the same sunny location, the white cup reached 26°C and the black cup reached 35°C. Both cups warmed, but the black cup warmed much faster. A reasonable claim is that the black cup absorbed more light energy from the Sun. The evidence is the larger temperature increase: the black cup warmed by 15°C, while the white cup warmed by 6°C. Good reasoning connects the evidence to the science idea that absorbed light energy can transform into thermal energy. To make the test fair, students should control water volume, starting temperature, cup material except color, sunlight exposure, location, and timing.
